newsitem.title: JAPAN: Minor Metals--Cobalt strong, upside seen limited.
newsitem.headline: Minor Metals--Cobalt strong, upside seen limited.

text.p: Cobalt prices rose as Zairean rebels tightened their grip on the country's key mining region, but the market was unlikely to climb much further, Asian traders said on Tuesday.

"Cobalt will remain strong unless something clears up the political uncertainties in Zaire," said a trader at a major Japanese trading house. "Zaire has suspended sales. We also hear that Falconbridge (Ltd) is sold out for April and May shipments."
Rebels in Zaire, a major cobalt producer, took over the capital of mineral-rich Shaba province last week and appointed a new governor there.
Traders said high-grade cobalt traded around $25 a lb and lower-grade Russian metal at $23 to $24.
Adding to uncertainties was a halt in U.S. stockpile cobalt shipments and sales. Stockpile deputy administrator Robert O'Brien said they would be suspended until at least April 28.

But traders in Tokyo said the scope for further price rises was limited as Zaire was unlikely to suspend sales of cobalt, a major source of hard currency, for very long. Major users could also start switching to substitutes if the price nears $30.
"End-users are not worried too much because at the moment we have enough stocks in Japan," one trader said. "It is traders who are bidding up the prices."
In the magnesium market, prices were unchanged at $2,350/2,450 per tonne, although Chinese suppliers would like to see price increases to cover their production costs, traders in Tokyo said.
One trader said, however, that the Japanese were reluctant to accept higher prices from China, as Japan's domestic prices had already been lifted by the weak yen.
A trader in Hong Kong said Chinese magnesium producers were selling old stock as prices remained flat.
"Margins are too low, there is too much material, competition is tough, producers are going broke, the EU is making dumping claims and there is a pile of paperwork to be done," he said.

Flat prices led to a rise in material being smuggled out of China to avoid taxes and charges, including a "resources protection fee" introduced about three years ago by Liaoning Province in northeast China that adds $45 a tonne to the price, he said.
"Just yesterday I heard about 10,000 tonnes of magnesite that was declared to customs as flint clay, because at customs they don't know what magnesite is," the trader said.

Traders in Tokyo said Russian offers of stockpiled magnesium were unlikely to have much impact in Asia. European traders said on Monday around 4,000 tonnes of Russian stockpiled magnesium was offered and there could be another 10,000 tones available.
"The metal should go to Europe and we will see it only indirectly. Europe's demand is rising and they might be able to absorb part of the additional supply," a trader said.
Japan's molybdenum oxide market was steady at $4.60/4.70 a lb, but bulls were gaining power, traders said.

"I would not be surprised if the price went up to five dollars," said one trader, adding that while demand was stronger than earlier expected, additional supply from Molycorp of the United States remained restricted.
In Shanghai, antimony prices had begun to soften, a trader with a European firm said.

"At the end of last week, someone dumped some material on the market," he said, adding that Chinese sellers were now quoting $2,350 a tonne. Chinese producers would be satisfied to see prices around $2,200 a tonne, he said.
Traders gave the following current prices for minor metals, on a CIF basis at major Japanese ports, except for antimony, which is FOB Southern China:
April 15 April 8
Molybdenum Oxide ($/lb) 4.60/4.70 4.60/4.70
Magnesium (Chinese, $/tonne) 2,350/2,450 2,350/2,450
